cells.tense: Right now you are holding several true weights and setting none of them down.
cells.act: join the practice the others keep
cells.ask: Turn up to that standing group you already belong to without waiting for an invitation, and change how you take part — come first if you usually come late, bring what nobody brings. Give it three weeks, including the weeks you feel least like matching anyone.
cells.core:
You read a room fast and move with it — adding here, easing off there — and that isn't peacekeeping. It's how you stay level, and it comes through as steadiness people settle around. Somebody is actually paying attention, and the room can feel it.

There's a standing thing you turn up to. Go next time without being invited, and shift how you take part — arrive first if you usually come late, bring what nobody brings. The others will clock the change and you'll still be one of them. A practice stays alive by passing through people and coming out slightly different each time. The difference is allowed, and it's usually the point.

cells.tense: You are bracing against a fight that hasn't happened yet and calling it peacemaking.
cells.act: move toward the thing you want, one step, today
cells.ask: Take the one honest move you've been holding — the true sentence, the actual request — today, before the room settles. No run-up. You'll learn what the not-saying was protecting, whether you wanted it or just wanted the politeness.
cells.core:
You are smoothing the room before anyone has said anything real. Differences get folded away so fast nobody has to feel them, and it reads as grace — nothing rattles, no one is caught out. But a merge nobody agreed to starts to look like a verdict that everything is already settled. You'd call it keeping the peace. What's happening is you getting to the end while the rest of the room is still reading.

Pick the one honest move you've been holding back: saying the true version, asking for the actual thing. Take it before the room settles, one move and no run-up. You won't know what it costs until it's done, and you'll know right away whether the want was real or just the polite one. Either answer is worth having.

cells.tense: You are still standing in a room you left, adjusting for people who aren't there.
cells.act: sit with someone in it without fixing it
cells.ask: Have someone you trust tell you about a hard stretch, and sit with it for a quarter of an hour changing nothing — no smoothing, no solution, no early exit. What you're practising is staying, not answering.
cells.core:
Too many rooms, and you're still turned toward all of them. You shift and adjust so constantly there's no fixed point left to shift around — even small choices get made and unmade until they stop being choices. The tuning runs; whatever it was tuning around has gone quiet. Nothing is wrong with you. This is just what a stretched system looks like from inside.

Sit with one person in something hard and do nothing about it. Not advice, not rescue — contact while it's difficult. A quarter of an hour, no exit. When you stop managing the room you're actually in, something in your own middle comes back online. You'll feel the difference by evening, and after a few days you'll know whether you want another round.

cells.tense: You are adjusting the mix minute to minute and keeping count of none of it.
cells.act: learn how the people before you did it
cells.ask: Find whoever taught you the thing you're good at and ask how they learned it and what they changed passing it on. Then run their older version once, even if yours works better.
cells.core:
You recalibrate constantly — pace, tone, how close to stand to something true — and if anyone asked, you'd shrug and say that's just how you are. The adjusting happens. That it's you doing it hasn't quite landed. Not because anything's missing; you've been inside it the whole time, and nobody told you to look for the author's name on the door.

Find whoever taught you the thing you're good at, and ask what they changed when they handed it on. One conversation. Then run their older version once, even if yours works better. You'll catch your own hand moving in a pattern older than you assumed, and that's how a thing gets carried — with a change in it, not despite one.
